subsubtopic: DOWNTURN IN SALES OF NORTH AMERICAN CARS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian auto industry has been hit hard by high interest rates and low priced imports. One third of Ontario auto dealers could be out of business in three months if action is not taken to halt the downturn in the sales of North American cars. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens):
That this House require the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to reassess current import levels and with his colleague, the Minister of Finance, take positive measures to reduce the crippling high interest rates that are now destroying the automobile industry, the dealers, and the jobs that go with them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Whereas it was clearly demontrated in yesterday's historical agreement that the great Liberal principles of our government and the prophetic vision of our Prime Minister, for which he has always fought, met the wishes and expectations of all Canadians; whereas it was also clear that the Premier of Quebec attended this conference with the sole purpose of scuttling it by committing what I would call political hijacking to serve separatist ends, and since our government's perceptiveness was once more clearly established, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and
November 6, 1981

pressing necessity. In view of the fact that a number of extremely plentiful species of wildlife have become extinct in Canada, and since, in fact, the planet is losing life forms at a rate of one species per day now which will accelerate to one species per hour by 1989 if mankind does not deal seriously with pollution and habitat protection, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), and I believe with the support of the government:
That this House urges the Minister of the Environment to move expeditiously with a wildlife policy for Canada which would include a mandate to protect the habitat of endangered species and, in co-operation with the provinces and territories, set aside world community ecological reserves and wildlife parks to preserve our precious global heritage.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT STATISTICS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As the minister I hope is aware, this morning Statistics Canada established the jobless rate at 8.3 per cent of the work force. That is 989,000 Canadians on the street and looking for work. In any language that is a staggering figure, and should be unacceptable to the government. Clearly it is the gover-ment's incompetence and lack of initiative which are responsible for this situation. When is the minister going to accept his responsibility for creating employment in this country and put those people back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been working actively to deal with the situation. I remind my hon. friend of major initiatives such as the 50 per cent increase in the funding for the Defence Industry Productivity Program, a major support program for
Oral Questions
the aerospace and electronics industry. I remind my hon. friend of initiatives under the special electronics program, individual projects such as support for de Havilland, in Toronto, and Pratt & Whitney in Montreal. There have been major announcements and major commitments and initiatives under my jurisdiction and that of other ministers. We have been working actively to create jobs and to stem the effects of economic situations in our major export markets. We will be continuing these initiatives. We are very much aware of the situation and of our responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, there may be major announcements, but they are certainly not major realities. The minister must be aware that the amount of unemployment has not only gone up but job creation has gone down. Last month employment creation by this government went down by 68,000 jobs. Statistics this morning show that job creation is down again for the second straight month-in manufacturing 22,000 jobs lost, in primary industries 16,000 jobs lost in one month alone. Surely the government is not proud of that record. This country is in a recession. Ordinary people are being hurt. They want to know in practical terms what the government is going to do about it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been a very strong and positive record of job creation for most of the period since this government took office, except for the most recent months. We are working-
No one else is.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: -to continue these efforts of job creation. My hon. friend has completely overlooked the fact of the very great degree of weakness and the high unemployment in our major export markets. The European community and the United States, for example, are areas that are bound to have an impact on job creation and industrial activity in our country. We are working to strengthen our export efforts and to strengthen job creation and industrial development in our own country. However, we cannot totally escape the impact of policies of other countries in their own markets and therefore on our industries. We are certainly conscious of these concerns and responsibilities, and are working to put in place other initiatives to help deal further with the impact of these matters on our workers.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the minister is aware that the statistics I have used this morning take us only to October 17. In the past three weeks we have had plant closings and lay-offs, putting thousands more people out of work. I can cite Du Pont, Alcan, Admiral and many small manufacturing companies across the country. Those people are no longer interested in the minister's

announcements or in blaming other people. They want to know what the minister and the government are waiting for. When are they going to do something of a practical nature that will help them out?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the previous questions I would like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. We have noticed over the last few weeks that there are 88,000 fewer jobs available in Canada. Today we see again that over the last month we have had an increase in the unemployment figures. When this session first began the Minister of Finance said that this high unemployment figure was an aberration, that perhaps it was a statistical error. Does the Prime Minister recognize that his
November 6, 1981

government's policy of maintaining high interest rates to stem spending in Canada is the major cause for these high unemployment figures?
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is confusing certain issues. By focusing only on the recent increase in unemployment rates he forgets to mention the fact that between October 1980 and October 1981, 170,000 jobs were created in Canada. He also forgets that high interest rates are directly linked to the high rate of inflation we are experiencing, and that it is not the government's task to concentrate on a single issue and on short-term requirements. Its task is to consider all economic indicators and to work towards improving the general state of the economy.

subsubtopic: SOCIAL COSTS OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us recognize that when the government talks about the jobs that have been created many of these jobs are recycled ones advertised through Manpower. They are not really new jobs being added to the economy.
My next question is aimed toward the minister responsible for unemployment-excuse me, employment. It seems to me that the government's policy of job creation as recently announced is the shifting of the unemployed from certain parts of Canada toward the megaprojects. Surely this will result in the uprooting and breakdown of families, resulting indirectly in family violence, wife battering, child abuse, drug and alcohol abuse, and the like.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister prepared to agree that this high unemployment results directly in these incredible social costs that will be with us for many decades?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: SOCIAL COSTS OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of unemployment is never a pleasant one and this government is very concerned about the measures we can introduce to try to alleviate it and help those who face this situation.
I would like to point out to the House that in the past year, just through the initiatives of our department alone, we have added something like 80,000 jobs which are concentrated particularly in those regions of the country that experience chronic unemployment.
Oral Questions
As far as the movement of Canadians is concerned, that is something that has been part and parcel of the history of this country. Every year some one half million Canadians move to take jobs in other areas. That is really part of the labour market. What we are trying to do is develop, through recommendations of the parliamentary task force and our own task forces, a whole new set of labour and training programs that will respond to the new labour demands of the 1980s. It is the real commitment of this government to address the issue of human resources and the labour market so we can address the kind of problems the hon. member points out as being a consequence of unemployment, and I believe that between the budget and the kinds of programs we are initiating we will be able to provide this country with a very relevant, very useful, and effective labour market strategy in the years to come.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FOREST INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my final question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Recognizing that he has taken initiatives on a number of occasions in an effort to assist certain sectors of the country and the economy, will he outline what he plans to do to provide assistance to the ailing British Columbia forest industry that is now experiencing lay-offs on a daily basis, with an unemployment rate for woodworkers in excess of 20 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA FOREST INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have a major program in place to assist the British Columbia forest industry, to develop additional markets in the world aside from the United States. This has had a major, positive impact. As I said in the House the other day, over the past few years it has brought about an increase in exports to other parts of the world from $200 million to close to $1 billion. We are continuing these efforts to assist the industry and to expand its export sales and help all its needs in terms of maintenance of employment in the British Columbia industry.
We are also working with the Department of Employment and Immigration on programs in terms of assisting laid off workers, and we look forward to further efforts to strengthen the base of that industry, despite the decline in major export markets, particularly in the United States, something that unfortunately is not within our direct control.

subsubtopic: PROVISION RESPECTING WOMEN'S RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister responsible for the status of women my question is for the Prime Minister. As the Prime Minister knows, Clause 28 of the constitutional resolution is a paramountcy clause outside the charter. I remind him that Clause 28 is the one saying
Notwithstanding anything in this Charter, the rights and freedoms referred to in it are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.
What I would like to ask the Prime Minister is if he can tell the House whether Clause 28 will continue to have paramountcy. That is, will it override any attempts made to deny equality to women?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat reluctant to raise a point of order today for the very reason that this is your first occasion in the chair during question period. However, when something is out of order, it is out of order. Unfortunately, today something was indeed out of order, in my judgment.
Today during motions, the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) rose and placed before you a motion under Standing Order 43. As you are aware, the first question put to the House asks for unanimous consent to waive the notice provision. That question was quite properly put to the House. The only obligation on the Chair at that point was to determine whether the Chair heard any dissenting voices. The Chair, in the wisdom of the Chair, did not hear any dissenting voices; therefore the motion was then read to the House. After the motion was read to the House, the Chair asked for unanimous consent to proceed with the motion. I put to you, Sir, that it is quite out of the ordinary and in fact unnecessary to obtain unanimous consent of the House at that point. All that is required at that point is for the Chair to put the motion, and then the motion is debated in the way of all other motions.
The fact that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) rose and claimed that he had refused unanimous consent is irrelevant and therefore cannot be taken into consideration by the Chair once the Chair has decided that it heard no dissenting voices.
I ask the Chair to review this procedure over the course of the weekend to determine whether or not the facts as I have presented them to the Chair-and in fact as they will appear in the "blues", since I have read them-are accurate; whether it is true that there is no need for unanimous consent for the motion to be considered by the House after the request for waiving of notice has been given; and whether in fact there

ought not to have been then an opportunity given to any member of the House to debate the motion.
I realize that one cannot go back into history and have the debate now; I am not asking for that. However, I am asking that the matter be clarified, that it be recognized-and I put it without malice-that in fact there was an error, and that the procedure be clarified for future consideration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
That Bill C-78, an act to provide for the payment of benefits to laid-off employees and to amend the Canada Labour Code, be read for the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise on the second reading of Bill C-78 designed to provide for the payment of benefits to laid-off employees and to amend the Canada Labour Code. The bill reflects Labour Canada's participation in the $350 million Industry and Labour Adjustment Program announced in January 1981 by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane), the Minister of Employment and

November 6, 1981
Labour Adjustment Benefits
Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and my predecessor, the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan). As most hon. members are already aware, the various aspects of the program being proposed in this bill are aimed at facilitating labour adjustment by increasing the responsibility of employers and government with respect to displaced employees. They also provide for increased participation of employees in the process of deciding on provisions for adjustment in case of lay-off.

The major features of this bill-authority to provide early retirement pensions to employees who are unable to obtain alternative employment; an innovative process for dealing fairly with mass terminations; and improvement in severance pay provisions-flow from measures already existing and from recent extensive consultations with business and unions, as well as from the unanimous report of a tripartite commission of inquiry headed by Professor Carrothers. The report was handed down in late 1979.
The early retirement program has been in operation for several years in the clothing industry, the textile industry and the footwear industry, based upon the authority of a previous Appropriation Act. This bill will permit the immediate extension of early retirement benefits to qualified persons in the communities of Windsor, Tracy-Sorel, Port Cartier, Sept Isles, Schefferville and Sydney, N.S., and to industries which have been, or are to be, designated under the industrial and labour adjustments program.
As the House is aware, some 500 persons are being assisted by the current program. While it is very regrettable when a firm in a vulnerable industry closes its doors or is forced to reduce its operations and persons are left without employment, the array of measures available under government programs- job creation, job finding, mobility, training and so forth- coupled with early retirement as a last resort, go a long way toward helping the affected worker. There are several communities where textile and clothing firms have folded under international trading pressures or economic circumstances and employees have found themselves jobless.
In most cases other government programs have been able to provide alternative employment in short order, but for those who cannot move, cannot find something else or cannot be retrained, at least at that point in time, the early retirement benefit is a measure which maintains income in a manner consistent with human dignity. At the same time, the government does not simply leave the person there unaided. Efforts continue to help the worker find other permanent employment or to create the necessary jobs.
Consider the case of a recent lay-off involving 52 people in a large textile plant in Drummondville. All the people laid off were over 54 years of age and, therefore, eligible for assistance under the former federal adjustment program. It helped people bridge the gap until such time as they found other employment or were eligible for pensions.
Now, an older worker who finds himself without a job through no fault of his own after working ten years in, say, an auto firm, who has exhausted his unemployment insurance benefits and yet is not eligible for pensions, will be able to call upon the labour adjustment benefits program for assistance.
The innovative process for dealing fairly with mass terminations stems from the provisions already in the Canada Labour Code requiring adequate notice to be given; but notice is not enough. As members will be aware, there have been several cases in the last couple of years where firms closed, leaving employees high and dry without termination benefits-severance pay, pension rights and buy-out of equity in their jobs. The result has been that employees engaged in strike action sometimes had virtually to occupy the plant in order to force justice out of their erstwhile employers.
This bill will require employers in the federal jurisdiction to negotiate a fair termination settlement package with their displaced employees or union. May I remind hon. members that the federal jurisdiction encompasses railways, trucking, shipping, banking, grain handling and other national infrastructure industries. It will provide that, in the absence of agreement, a third party will make a final and binding decision that will eliminate the necessity for employees to engage in desperate measures of "industrial action" in order to uphold their rights.
The measure we are proposing today is something unique in Canada and probably in North America at this point. I believe it will bring justice to persons caught up in mass terminations caused by economic and technological change. Enlightened and socially responsible employers are already pursuing this kind of process when forced to curtail operations.
I believe this bill is sound, desirable and in the interest of Canadian workers, and I urge members on all sides of this House to support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say that I am very pleased to be able to speak to this bill. In particular, because of its being introduced by an old friend and colleague, I would like to congratulate the new minister on his first bill in this House.
When the matter goes to committee, we on this side of the House will be asking some questions and proposing some changes of a technical nature, particularly relating to appointments and some other matters. Also in committee we will be raising the question of coverage. I am sure it is no surprise to the minister that this bill will not have a very good effect with respect to classes of workers that he has in mind who are women. By the very nature of their jobs and employment record over the last 20 years, women will not find the same kind of coverage as male workers.
Let me state clearly it is not a responsibility of the minister in that regard, but it is something to which he may want to give further consideration. There is a clause of the bill which allows for greater flexibility by the board in certain cases. The minister may want to give some consideration to expansion of that clause so that it clearly states the board will be able to
November 6, 1981

deal more equitably with regard to women workers in the work force.
My comments today are going to deal primarily with the problem that the bill is intended to deal with, not in the past but in the future. With great respect to my colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia), this bill looks at what the problem has been and is right now. It does very little to deal with what is increasingly a very fast growing scene with respect to employment, unemployment and job creation in this country.
It is interesting that the bill should be dealt with today when the unemployment and job-creation statistics came from Statistics Canada. It is worth referring to the unemployment problem and the job problem in this country. This bill is a fairly puny attempt at trying to deal with what the minister is pleased to call an assault on technological change in this country.	-
The unemployment rate in this country is now at 8.3 per cent. That means that on a seasonally adjusted basis we now have, as recorded up to October 17, 989,000 Canadians out of work. If I just left it there, it would be an awesome enough figure for members on all sides to consider when looking at the specific individual misery that causes. However, if I look at it a little more closely, I see that it affects particular groups even more so. Unfortunately, these groups are not covered in any significant way by the bill. The hardest hit group are young people between the ages of 15 and 24. This month alone there are 32,000 people in this age group who are unemployed and have lost their jobs in one month's time. There are 99,000 fewer jobs than in June 1981 for this group, and 44 per cent, almost half, of the 989,000 unemployed are between the ages of 15 and 24.
It is indeed a terrible thing at an advanced age to find yourself unemployed because it speaks to how you feel about yourself and your family, how they feel about you, your standing in the community and your sense of worth. It is a different experience but just as miserable for a person who is just starting out to find that one of every two who looks for a job will not find one.
That is the situation the government has us in today. Putting aside those people between the ages of 15 and 24 looking at geographic reasons, the province of Quebec lost 9,000 jobs last month alone. Unemployment in the province of Quebec is now at 11.5 per cent. That is the highest unemployment rate for that province in modern times. Of those entering the labour force over the past year, 44 per cent were unable to find a job. One further statistic shows that 132,000 fewer people are working today compared to this times last year.
In spite of comments being made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), about job creation, the reality is in fact the reverse. Unemployment has risen and job creation has fallen. Those are the facts. All the words from
Labour Adjustment Benefits
ministers of the Crown will not change that reality for the Canadians who are suffering.
We agree that this bill should have been brought forward some time ago. But for those people who are in their fifties who will be laid off as a consequence of a depressed industry, and looking at the total situation with respect to employment opportunities in this country, this bill is indeed far, far too late. It is neither very strong nor very effective for the great majority of the people who will be affected.
The minister also spoke of technological change. I wish he had not said that because he at least shows that his department has some nodding acquaintance that we have been in a technological revolution for some time. It is that technological revolution which the minister is not taking into account in this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer some thoughts today to the minister and his department with respect to this bill. Both he and the Minister of Employment and Immigration have certainly demonstrated no action with respect to placing this country in a position of competitiveness in the face of technological change and they have spent precious little time on it. For the past 20 years the minister's colleagues have been putting their heads in the sand about what is going on in this world concerning technological change. That is the reason the minister brought this bill forward.
We are in the midst of a revolution of scientific, economic and technological dimensions which will change forever the work place in Canada. Our productivity and competitiveness as a nation and our relations with one another as human beings will be changed. Let me use one example of that change which is already about us. I think of robots because that is perhaps the most dramatic and obvious example, particularly if one thinks of their utilization in factories. Already in the world there are robots that can paint cars, command milling machines, weld auto parts, hoist turbine blades, pack candies, wash windows, and in Australia robots shear sheep.
We must remember that robots never go on strike, they never call in sick, they work double shifts without complaint, they never file insurance claims or go on vacations and they

November 6, 1981
Labour Adjustment Benefits
work well in hostile environments. There are approximately
15,000	robots in Japan, approximately 4,000 in the United States and approximately 5,000 in Germany. There are precious few in Canada. But more importantly, when those changes come, and come they will, the best the government can do with respect to technological change is to deal only with those people who are in industries that are being depressed by government policies and only those people who are in their mid-fifties. That help is needed but it shows that the government is totally ill equipped to deal with the technological change that is coming upon this country.
The growth and development of the Canadian economy in the 1980s, the 1990s and into the twenty-first century will require a fundamental change in our educational opportunities, our scientific research, our technology and technological education and in our human resources development. Specifically as a nation we will need to develop policies that will take us in those directions.
Education, for example, is a provincial responsibility. It is also a national concern. It was announced by the Minister of Finance and then I think denounced by another minister the other day that this government would cut $1.5 billion out of the established programs financing in federal aid to education. That act alone shows that the government has no understanding of the role educational institutions have to play in relation to technological change so that we will not have the unemployed people the Minister of Labour is trying to protect. Educational institutions depend fundamentally on federal aid. Forty-five per cent of the operating costs of universities in this country is provided by the federal government. If the Minister of Finance has his way, educational institutions will find themselves in very great difficulty. That difficulty will further expand the already terrible situation for young people who are between the ages of 15 and 24 years, among whom already almost one out of every two are without jobs.
We should begin to provide leadership, and I hope that the federal government will offer leadership in this regard, although I do not see anything that tells me that the federal government will do so, in co-operation with the provinces, regarding the equalization of educational opportunity in this country. We need to ensure the existence of world class institutions of advanced education in particular fields. We need support for world class programs in research, both basic and applied. We have to ensure high-level technology training to develop people with world class skills and abilities. We have to provide support for unique and fundamentally important resources, such as archives, museums, rare books and scholarship programs.
When I hear the minister talk about attempting to deal with technological change, and when I hear his colleagues talk about their concerns with respect to policies of cutting back on aid to education, it shows me again that the government will not take us into the future but back to 1960. This country has to equip itself for the 1980s, the 1990s and the twenty-first century. The policies which the government is proposing will not bring us the excellence we need. Indeed, these policies will
maintain the mediocrity which the government has imposed when it comes to research and development in Canada.
The bill itself, as I indicated earlier, is one which we will deal with in committee in terms of its specifics. I indicated that one of the specifics was that of the problems women face in the work force. The difficulty is that the regulations imposed by the legislation are such that most women, given the fact that many are regarded as playing an important role in raising children within the household, together with the kinds of jobs they have been forced into over the last number of years, will not have work opportunities. This is a problem in respect of which I hope the minister will take us into his confidence in committee so that we can see whether he is willing to expand that section which deals with the discretion the board will have.
The matter I dealt with a moment ago with respect to technological change is one with which I am hoping the Minister of Labour will be able to deal. The Minister of Employment and Immigration so far has failed to do anything of a significant nature for us. Clearly the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce likes to talk only about announcing programs without putting them into effect. The Minister of Labour has a unique opportunity because, as a new minister, he can carve out new opportunities and grounds in relation to his own responsibility. This is clearly a situation where responsibility is going from one minister to another, and for very good reason. I think the new minister may be able to do something the former minister could not.
When the new minister is dealing with his colleagues he may want to look again at policy with respect to the established programs financing. I dwell on this because the established programs financing, which was established in 1977, as the minister may recall, was to allow flexibility in programs for provincial administration while at the same time putting a cap on committed federal government expenditures. That was the result of a request, interestingly enough, made by the federal government.
Up until 1977 federal aid to education, hospital insurance and medical care was handled on a cost-share basis. That was not acceptable to the federal government because it wished to have some control over its expenditures, and it was becoming increasingly unacceptable to the provinces because they found themselves having to live within criteria they did not want as established by the federal government. Both sides decided in 1977 that it was of mutual benefit to make a change in the way in which moneys flowed from the federal government to the provinces.
That change came about in 1977 under what was called established programs financing. What it established was that under those programs in education, hospital insurance and medical care the provinces would get a lump sum of money or a block fund, an amount to be determined by the relationship of the province to the increase in the gross national product.
November 6, 1981

I emphasize this because the government in the past two years, certainly in the last year and a half, rather than dealing with our real problems has sought to blame the provinces for not carrying out what this government was pleased to call the provinces' responsibilities with respect to education and medical care.
The fact of the matter is that it was the federal government that asked for the change. Any reading of the words of the then minister responsible, who is now the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), and indeed, a reading of a speech of the Prime Minister of the time, will show they extolled the virtues of the established programs financing because it gave the very flexibility for which they now condemn the provincial governments.
I am one who is interested in having the provinces of this country contribute more in the field of education. We need not less money from the federal government for education, research and development, but more. There are a number of sins this government has committed over the past ten years in respect of education for which it will have to fess up. One of the things it will have to make sure it discontinues is blaming the provinces without putting up the money and the leadership.
Every educational institution, every corporation interested in on-the-job training, every province that is interested in apprenticeship training and every school that is interested in technical training is looking for leadership. This is not the kind of leadership that means the federal government collects the money, spends the money and therefore controls it centrally. The great difficulty we have had so far with this government is that every time it contributes money it thinks it ought to control the policies relating to it. That is not the way our federalism works. I have noted in the past few days that a number of people have begun to understand how the federal system actually does work, and that is why so many of us were pleased the other night. One of the things this government ought to remember is that although the parochialists may be bad, the centralizers are just as bad.
When it comes to providing money for employment, research and development and education, this is done best at a local level. Small and medium-size business in this country create more than half the jobs, and the important relationship between small and medium-size businesses is their relationship to the municipalities, the regions and the provinces in which they exist. If the federal government thinks that by the power of the purse it is going to create educational programs for this country, it is wrong. That is not the kind of leadership the country needs. The leadership must come as a result of a co-operative endeavour between the provinces and the federal government. The existing council of ministers of education needs to be expanded. I might say that two parliamentary committees have already reported and have attempted to make sure that the federal government, first of all, does not cut out the $1.5 billion federal aid to education, and second, that the federal government understands that in its endeavours its leadership is required to make sure local areas are getting the funds. It must provide the leadership to make sure that the
Labour Adjustment Benefits
provinces, regions, municipalities and local areas are able to work with small and medium-size businesses in their own areas.
I continue to emphasize leadership because we have had so little from the federal government in this field for so long. That is why many other countries which we previously regarded as being behind us in the technological field, in education, in productivity, in competitiveness and in standard of living, are now ahead of us. They are ahead of us because we constantly see bills from this government dealing with real problems that could have been solved earlier.

speechtext:
My hon. friend asks why not by the provinces. In the three years I have been here I have heard minister after minister on the government side, except for a nine-month period, constantly state that our problems are the fault of somebody else. I have heard them blame the provinces and world conditions. All other countries live in the same world, yet we have gone from second place in terms of competitiveness and standard of living to somewhere around fourteenth. The fact of the matter is that the federal government has allowed this country to forget that we established our standard of living in this twentieth century through a belief in the validity of science and the ability of human beings to acquire research and development techniques to exploit science for economic development. That is the kernel of what we are talking about.
When the minister talks about technological change, all he is talking about is what we were involved in many years ago. That is, the realization that the only way in which we progress in this world in economic development is through science, research and development and on-the-job training. All of that has been lost.
In 1951, the Massey commission advised the government of that time that its role in economic development, particularly related to technical and technological education, was not only important but crucial. That was 30 years ago. In 1951, the Massey commission said that the federal government must continue the same aid which it had provided in the 1940s during the war, and late in the 1940s for employment rehabilitation for people who came back from overseas.
In 1940, this country took its first step as a federal government in the field of technological education. It expanded and intensified it during the 1940s. In 1951 when Mr. Massey recommended it be expanded again, we did so for about three years.
Interestingly enough, I offer this as a non-partisan thought, which it is. It expanded again in 1958, 1959 and 1960, when federal aid was expanded to technical and technological institutions in this country. It closed down again in the mid-1960s and it has become worse throughout the 1970s, a whole decade. There has been no fresh program for a whole decade, indeed no fresh thought by the Liberal governments we have

had, on how we move the country back into international competitiveness, with excellence rather than mediocrity in our research and development as our major criteria.

Mr. Speaker, members of our party look upon any proposal to create a labour adjustment assistance program as one which will only have any real merit or relevance if it is part of a planned objective and policy which takes into account the needs of workers in a particular industry. It will only work when we have as our objective the establishment of the principle that every person in this country who wants to work is able to find a job.
It is interesting-coincidental, of course-that the minister brings forth this bill on the same day that Statistics Canada produces the grim report that approximately 989,000 Canadians are unemployed. That means 8.2 per cent of the work force across this country are out of work. The minister should remember that that figure of 989,000 is not the factual figure. The real figure is substantially higher, probably 1,300,000 who are unemployed. The reason the figure is higher-and this was mentioned during question period today-is that the figures calculated by Statistics Canada do not include the tens of thousands of native people living on reserves where the unemployment rate is anywhere from 60 per cent to 90 per cent for a good part of the year. It does not include the tens of thousands of people in slow growth areas such as Atlantic Canada, the Gaspe Peninsula and certain parts of Manitoba where jobs are so few that thousands of people who want work have simply given up looking. speechtext:
My colleague from Beaches in Toronto mentions the disabled.
I was a member of the parliamentary task force on Employment for the '80s which looked at the prospects for employment for approximately the next ten years. The task force, which was made up of four members from the Liberal Party, two Conservative members and myself from the New Democratic Party, studied the question of employment and listened to people from one end of the country to the other, people at the grass roots level. We considered the problems of unemployment, why there was unemployment, and then gave consideration to the question of full employment.
I do not do this often, but I want to put on record a few sections of that report. I do this, Mr. Speaker, because it is not unusual for members of this House to hear members of our party, including myself, say that it is not only possible but imperative that we adopt policies that would permit every person in Canada who wants to work to be gainfully employed.
Here we have a report signed and supported, but for a couple of very small reservations, by the two Conservative members and approved by the four Liberal members which deals specifically with the whole question of full employment, without which I think what the minister is bringing forward today is really an exercise in futility. In saying that I am being very charitable to the minister.
Let me now put on the record a few paragraphs from this report:
Task force members did not accept that there was no solution to the present trade-offs between high unemployment on the one hand and high inflation on the other. They felt that human ingenuity and political will should provide better solutions.
The Liberal members agreed to that. It then goes on to quote from a white paper on employment and income issued in 1945 by a Liberal government. That report said:
The Government has stated unequivocally its adoption of a high and stable level of employment and income, and thereby higher standards of living, as a major aim of Government policy. It has been made clear that, if it is to be achieved, the endeavour to achieve it must pervade all government economic policy. It must be wholeheartedly accepted by all economic groups and organizations as a great national objective, transcending in importance all sectional and group interests.
If there is one group that seems to have forgotten that important recommendation of the white paper, it is the Liberal government of 1981 which is ignoring the advice of the Liberal government of 1945.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before we terminated the debate at one o'clock I put on the record the central principle of the white paper tabled just after World War II by that most eminent Liberal cabinet minister of the day, C. D. Howe, which was that that Liberal government committed itself to work toward full employment. When it was established, the Economic Council set its goal in its first annual report in 1964. With regard to employment the report said, and I quote:
-a calculation of the possible,... a target to be aimed at,... not the highest level of attainment under the best of all possible circumstances, but rather an indicator of productive capabilities under reasonable expectations of performance.
With this in mind the council projected that a 97 per cent rate of employment, or a 3 per cent rate of unemployment in the labour force, would be a realistic objective.
For a number of years between the mid-1960s and 1967 we actually had an unemployment rate of just 3.8 per cent. However, in the 1970s that 3 per cent target disappeared. Indeed, when the Liberal government passed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in 1971, it based its legislation on the principle that the average unemployment would be 4 per cent and that over the 4 per cent rate the government would pick up the deficits which would be created in payments of unemployment insurance benefits.
In recent years the government seems to have moved away from earlier ideas about full employment. The Governor of the Bank of Canada has suggested that there is full employment when we have 7 per cent or 8 per cent unemployment. In the budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) introduced in November of 1980 he projected-and accepted-an unemployment rate in excess of 8 per cent for the first five years of the 1980s. I point out that this is double the 4 per cent rate the government found acceptable in 1971.
Given these facts and the fact I pointed out when I began my speech, that the official rate of unemployment accepted by Statistics Canada-which, if anything, underestimates the amount of unemployment we have-is now 8.4 per cent, the task force which, as I pointed out, had a majority of members who were Liberals and was chaired by a former cabinet minister, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), said in connection with the question of full employment-I just want to put this last paragraph on the record:
Canada needs an industrial strategy that will put people to work, and a government determined to achieve this goal must set goals for lowering unemployment. This strategy should aim to achieve full employment, which the task force considers to be 4 per cent unemployment. Government policy should be designed to meet this goal as soon as possible.
One can see how far the policies adopted by the government are from the objective set out by that task force in which Liberal members were very heavily involved.
What we have in the bill proposed by the minister today is supposedly an adjustment assistance program, but it is a program which excludes nearly all the people who lose their jobs. I will not go into the details now. Some of my colleagues will follow in the debate a little later, but the program excludes people who have worked less than ten years and
Labour Adjustment Benefits
people who are not yet in their fifties. I am sure that if the bill were in effect now, virtually none of the 2,000 people who received their lay-off notices yesterday when the Admiral Corporation closed down would have been eligible for assistance.
We reject this very picayune approach of the government. We believe that an adjustment program, as I said earlier, must be part of a strategy designed to give employment to all those who want to work. If people are unemployed, then the adjustment program, along with the other programs we have such as unemployment insurance, must assure assistance to people laid off through no fault of their own, to a large extent because of the mistaken economic policies of the government and the high interest rate policies adopted by this government which have created situations where there are no sales for the companies for which they work.
With interest rates at 20 per cent for housing mortgages, it is not surprising that tens of thousands of workers in the forest industry are unemployed. And with housing sales plummeting to near zero, it is not surprising that Canadian citizens are not buying appliances. That is the reason the Admiral Corporation had no customers for its product. It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that the automobile industry is in such dire straits.
Given that situation, what does the minister propose in the bill? First to qualify you must be a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident, have been laid off as a result of non-cyclical factors, the total lay-off must equal 10 per cent of employees or 50 employees. You must also have been employed for 10 years out of the past 15 years in the industry, be 54 to 65 years of age, exhausted you unemployment insurance benefits and have no prospects for employment or are able to find only a low paying job.
What the government's objective was when it drafted this bill, Mr. Speaker, was to find ways to exclude as many people as it could, rather than design a bill that would include as many people as possible who need protection because they have been laid off.
It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that various groups of people, groups like the Canadian Labour Congress, individual unions and people in academic positions, people concerned about the welfare of their fellow Canadians, not only think this bill is totally inadequate but have drafted or have started to draft real alternatives that would help such people.
For more than a year, Mr. Speaker, I have worked on a private member's bill that would deal with the question of plant closures or cutbacks and with the plight of people who are laid off. This bill, Mr. Speaker, is almost ready. As far as I am concerned, it is ready but it has to be approved by the legal experts of the House of Commons. As soon as it is, I intend to introduce it.
My bill, unlike this bill, Mr. Speaker, will go a long way to mitigate the serious consequences of lay-offs. My bill includes appropriate time frames for notices of termination, which this bill does not deal with. I start with the principle that it is not

November 6, 1981
Labour Adjustment Benefits
acceptable that an employer can decide in a day, week, or month's notice that the business shall close and that his employees who have worked for many years will be thrown on the breadline or will have to depend on unemployment insurance. I do not believe that one or two weeks' notice or even one day's notice is enough. This occurs too frequently. I believe such short notices give the employees little, if any, opportunity to prepare for and to obtain new employment.
I know the minister knows that what I am proposing in this bill is close to what the organizations, such as the Canadian Labour Congress, have proposed. I am suggesting that employers be required to give 26 weeks' notice to the employees when they are terminating their work, where there are less than 50 employees involved, and 52 weeks' notice where there are 50 or more employees who will be laid off.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
I am suggesting in all instances of temporary lay-offs that the employer be required to give one month's notice and continue to pay all benefits, such as health insurance, pension and so on, contracted by the employees with the employer for the duration of the lay-off. Too many employees find themselves in difficulty where they are laid off for one, two or three months and cannot make up the benefits they have lost during that period.
Where the duration of unemployment is lengthy, I am suggesting that the employee should receive at least one week's severance pay for each year of service, and that pensions should be made more portable than they have up until now. Thousands of employees in this country lose the benefits of those pensions they have contributed to because the companies they work for do not work for them and the employees have to seek other employment whereby their pensions are not portable. I propose that pension contributions be placed in a central pension agency until retirement of the affected employees, or until the employees become a member of another plan. The funds would then be transferred to a new plan.
Where the duration of employment with employees is the result of the introduction of new equipment, I am suggesting that a labour-management committee be set up, consisting of an equal number of members from labour and management, to monitor the production of the new equipment, procedures and problems associated with the same. I suggest to the minister that if that kind of board had been set up in the post office, we would have avoided the difficulties we had over the last ten years because the employees would have had assurances and guarantees that the automation installed in the post office would not displace them from the jobs they held.
Mass terminations obviously create the greatest social and economic hardship and dislocation. Therefore, a permanent job protection board should be established to investigate employment terminations involving 50 or more employees and all permanent business closures. The board should also be permitted to investigate terminations of employment involving less than 50 employees when it is warranted. The business involved would be compelled to provide market and financial
information as required by the board and the board would have all the powers included in the Inquiries Act so as to ensure that the workers are not mistreated for reasons beyond their control. I suggest the board would make recommendations as to whether terminations are justified and what actions and remedies are required. These recommendations would be submitted to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) at least 90 days before the closing date set out in the termination notice.
The minister would then make orders, based on the board's recommendations, to reduce the impact of the employment terminations on the employees and communities. These orders would be made at least 60 days prior to the closing date set out in the termination notice.
I could continue, Mr. Speaker, but I think other members are interested in this subject because we are talking about the way of life of a large number of people, many of whom have worked for companies for 10, 15, 20 or 25 years and suddenly find themselves at the age of 40, 45, 50 or 55 where they have lost their jobs and are not able to find another job at all, or only find unskilled jobs or jobs that pay little more than the minimum wage.
If hon. members were to compare the kind of proposal that I am suggesting with the proposals contained in this bill, I think that those who look at it with a partial eye will see there is virtually nothing in the bill proposed by the government to give real protection to the workers.
As a matter of fact, it is interesting to note that the benefits which will be paid under the provisions of this bill to the few workers who might qualify will be even less than those paid to workers who have been laid off and are receiving compensation under the provisions of the bill we passed which gave some form of help to workers in the textile and clothing industry. Rather than the government improving and expanding the kind of legislation which began in the textile industry and the kind of legislation which at one time helped auto workers with transitional assistance benefits-and we need to improve them today given the fact that unemployment has risen so dramatically compared with what it was five or ten years ago-the government is cutting back on the meagre programs started a few years ago.
That being the situation, it is the intention of hon. members of the New Democratic Party to speak out and campaign as vigorously as we can against the half-baked, milquetoast proposal before us today and to vote against Bill C-78.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased at being able to take part in the debate on Bill C-78 now before the House, a bill announcing the implementation of the industrial and labour adjustment program. As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia), I wish to congratulate
November 6, 1981

the minister for insisting on having this bill passed as soon as possible, particularly in view of the present economic situation. It is the minister's first bill in the House. It is a good bill which will considerably improve the quality of benefits already being granted by the government to workers affected by employment slowdowns in a given sector.
Mr. Speaker, last January at a press conference in Sorel, Quebec, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) announced to hundreds of shipyard workers who had been affected by a considerable work slowdown that the federal government would help them by setting up a special industrial and labour adjustment program with a $350 million budget. Four other regions also designated on this occasion were Port-Cartier, Sept-Ues, Sydney, N.S. and Windsor. Mr. Speaker, the announcement could not have been made at a more appropriate time, because in my constituency, which is just opposite Sorel on the North Shore of the St. Lawrence, several hundred people work in the shipyards and their job situation has been seriously affected by lay-offs. And, Mr. Speaker, in other municipalities in the riding of Berthier-Mas-kinonge-Lanaudiere which I represent, the formerly flourishing textile industry was seriously affected by the slump in this sector and by the fact that a number of companies, including Associated Textiles of Canada Limited in Louiseville, which had over 600 employees, many of whom with more than 35 years' service, had to close down. This was quite a shock to the people in the area. I am very pleased that the government followed one of my recommendations by reducing the preretirement age from 54 to 50 for workers with 30 years' service in the same industry.
The various sections of the program provided under Bill C-78 are aimed at reducing the negative impact of the adjustment on wages, by increasing the responsibility of employers and government in this respect. Mr. Speaker, I would like to see the section of the act which sets at 50 the age requirement for pre-retirement applied retroactively, so as to cover under this act all workers who have lost their jobs in situations similar to the one I have just described, workers with more than 30 years' service and who were unable to receive preretirement pension benefits because they were not 54 years old at the time.
The labour adjustment benefits act is designed to make effective programs and policies aimed at helping employees to adjust to structural change by increasing the responsibility of both employers and government regarding workers affected by the adjustment. The act consists of two main parts: The first part, the labour adjustment benefits program, will provide pre-retirement benefits to older workers with a number of years of experience in the activity sectors affected by structural change. The second part of the act consists of amendments to Part III of the Canada Labour Code and will increase the rights of workers affected by collective lay-offs in activity sectors under federal jurisdiction. Both parts come under the $350 million Industry and Labour Adjustment Program
Labour Adjustment Benefits
announced by the government on January 19, 1981. Under the program, once the bill is passed, pre-retirement benefits will be paid to workers in designated communities. According to this bill, adjustment benefits already paid to workers in some industries under existing programs of adjustment benefits will continue to be paid.
Mr. Speaker, the program of adjustment benefits is aimed at providing, as a last resort, some financial assistance to older workers who have been laid-off in designated industries and who do not meet the requirements of other programs for a greater use of manpower. The industries involved are those where imports could give rise to a strong competition or those which are encouraged by the government through its programs and policies to undertake an industrial restructuring. In case of economic pressures, the cabinet could also designate industries in some special geographic areas. Those adjustment benefits granted on the basis of areas come under a program of assistance for the adjustment of industry and manpower announced in January 1981. Moreover, the program provides for the establishment of a Labour Adjustment Review Board to confirm the eligibility of certified workers to benefits. Indidivual applications will be processed by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. This program is a substitute for programs of adjustment benefits made available by the Department of Labour to workers in the textile, clothing and footwear industries.
To be eligible for benefits the employee will have to get the Labour Adjustment Review Board to confirm that he has been laid off; in other words, it must be certified that the lay-offs involve an establishment which belongs to a designated industry and affect 10 per cent of the manpower or 50 workers of the establishment, whichever is the lesser. The board must also be convinced that the lay-offs stem from a serious economic upheaval in the industry. To be entitled to labour adjustment benefits, Mr. Speaker, the applicant must be at least 54 but under 65 at the time of the lay-off, have exhausted all his unemployment insurance benefits, have at least ten years' employment in the industry in the 15 years immediately preceding the lay-off, be a Canadian citizen residing in Canada or a permanent resident, and have received from the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission a certificate attesting that the applicant has absolutely no employment opportunities or holds a job for which he is not paid as much as he was in his previous employment in the industry. Special attention might be paid to people aged 50 or over with 30 years of service in the industry at the time of the lay-off. Mr. Speaker, this is where I will ask that, if possible, this clause of the bill be made retroactive to the beginning of this program. The entitlement of workers to the labour adjustment benefits will be reviewed regularly by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. The benefits are equal to 60 per cent of the average insurable earnings before the lay-off. For 1981, the maximum insurable earnings prescribed under the Unemployment Insurance Act stand at $315-week, therefore

November 6, 1981
Labour Adjustment Benefits
the maximum labour adjustment benefits is $189 a week. They are reduced by 60 cents for each $1 of income from employment while the worker is registered under the program, and $1 for each $1 of income from another government transfer payment or from employment preceding the benefit period. The benefits will be indexed once a year to the cost of living.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the labour adjustment benefits act is mostly to provide last resort financial assistance to older workers who have been definitely laid off in designated industries and who do not meet the requirements for more active labour use programs. These industries are those where imports can create strong competition or those for which the government has incentive programs. In cases of serious economic pressures, the Cabinet can also designate, as I noted earlier, industries in specific geographic areas. These regional adjustment benefits are part of the industry and labour adjustment program.
The act also provides for the creation of a labour adjustment review board to certify the entitlement to benefits of laid-off workers. Individual claims are processed by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. Within a maximum limit provided by the act, a claimant can receive benefits equal to about 60 per cent of his average salary before his lay-off. The act currently covers adjustment benefit programs offered by the Department of Labour to the workers of the textile, clothing and footwear industries.
The proposed amendments to Part III of the Canada Labour Code aim at reducing the impact of termination of employment. The workers affected will be entitled to severance pay after one year of employment rather than five as is now the case. The employee will continue to receive two days wages for each completed year of employment. However, a minimum of five days wages will be provided and the maximum of 40 days wages now in effect will no longer apply. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, when the lay-off list includes 50 or more employees, the employer will have to give a 16 weeks notice and to establish a management-labour committee whose members will be responsible for developing a plan to minimize the impact of termination of employment. Under certain provisions, the minister will be able to appoint an arbitrator to settle disputes during the planning stage. If both parties are bound by a collective agreement which sets down the procedure to follow in the case of a mass lay-off, the employer will be exempted from having to establish the planning committee. Finally, the minister can waive the obligation of providing a notice or of having consultations when he is convinced that there already exists an orderly plan for termination of employment. Mr. Speaker, this legislation is of major interest to our workers and I hope that the House will give it the required support to ensure its speedy passage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this particular bill although it is not one to which I would normally turn my attention. In the past I have worked with the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and with what you might call more management oriented interests. Things have now reached the point where a properly trained labour supply has to become an integral part of management interests. It is an interest of government, of course.
Because of the developing nature of world industry we are faced with massive changes. For instance, in the petrochemical industry and other industries in this country we are dealing with world-scale plans. It is not only in that sector that one gets this massive type of installation but in the automobile industry, the farm machine industry, the textile, furniture and footwear industries. With the concentration of production in bigger and bigger operations, negative movements or events which force the closure of any particular plant will obviously mean massive lay-offs.
I think all of us will accept that the social impact of massive lay-offs in a community is not debatable. We all realize how difficult they are. One cannot say that a person who has taken employment with a particular firm in a particular industry has an inherent right to that job in the labour stream for life. There is no such thing as the acquired right to any particular job. There is movement in the labour force. After all, if the worker says that he or she has an acquired right to any particular job, then the employer in return may say there is also a required responsibility to furnish his or her labour in that particular industry. I am sure that not one person in this assembly would say that the worker should not be free, if he or she decides for one reason or another, capricious or otherwise, in a free country such as ours and indeed in a good part of the world, to withdraw their services and work elsewhere. There is a quid pro quo.
In the last five years in Canada, particularly in the furniture, textile and footwear industries in central Canada, this has become a problem although it may have been around a little longer than that. It is a particularly difficult situation in one industry towns as is the case in so much of rural Quebec and rural Ontario. A family business may have grown and been operated successfully, employing several hundred people. Then, for some reason or other, such as a change in technology or an obsolescent plant, the family-operated business is bought out by interests foreign to that community. This may just have meant a larger concern from elsewhere in Canada was buying up a branch in order to consolidate.
One of the reasons for the sale of family businesses in Quebec and Ontario was the almost predatory appetite of the provincial departments of finance to impose confiscatory death duties. There was no way that a family could face the death of the head of the family and the head of the business without having arranged the sale of the business beforehand in order to have the available cash to pay the death duties. The family
November 6, 1981

could not possibly arrange the financing. It sold to the highest bidder simply to put the principal owner of the industry in a position to deal with that day when the government's succession duty or estate duty people descended upon the family fortune. Therefore, we got these lay-offs.
Today the problem is much greater. We have announcements by Massey-Ferguson and the various automobile companies that they are laying off this or that number of employees. In many instances it is a permanent lay-off, not just a temporary reduction while liquidating inventory. It involves the closing of a plant.
How do we protect the workers in that situation? First, there must be between the federal and provincial governments some kind of retraining scheme made available to younger workers. Second, there should be the possibility of a transfer of workers to other plants or concerns in that industry. Third, with repetitive type of work which mechanization in industry has produced, you get premature aging manifested in many ways and encouragement toward earlier retirement of an individual.
It may be asked who is going to pay the cost. Let us look at society itself. I will use the example of a person who has reached age 55 and cannot work. The alternative to putting that person on a reasonable pension and keeping him or her in the home, true enough on a somewhat lesser scale than prior to the closure, unfortunately is simply to let that person fend for himself or herself until they fall on public assistance. Then the cost becomes entirely that of the public. The cost, not only financially but socially, of that person having been prematurely tossed on the scrapheap is far greater than arranging earlier retirement.
It is the same in business. An executive at the age of 60 may not be up to full production. He can cause more damage in either arriving at a decision or making a bad decision or decisions than what it would cost for that individual to retire early. He could be told that it is time he stepped aside, that someone younger and more able should take on the responsibility of the job. The company could tell him what they are prepared to pay him and the individual would have to arrange things beyond that. He could do something that interests him or something more in keeping with his diminished capabilities. It is a fact of life one has to meet.
When this bill was drafted, it was in the light of information on economic conditions that have long passed from viability. We said earlier that we would give this bill quick and enthusiastic passage. That is not so. My colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), indicated that conditions are such that during the past year this government has almost been mesmerized with patriation of the Constitution. There is no doubt that from October of last year until now this government has been preoccupied with non-economic conditions. The net result is that we have inflation running higher than ever, interest rates higher than ever before and 890,000 unemployed. This bill is a reflection of that limited thinking.

We see socialism. We have the whole of the British automobile industry in a socialized enterprise going on strike because the workers want everything. They are not interested in the continuation of the industry. The industry is inefficient. We see more and more industries being run by labour or socialized which should never be socialized. The record speaks for itself. It stinks. We will just lay that canard to rest right away.
I want to propose better training. A short time ago we had an industry and management task force study the work force that will be required with the fantastic expansion of the electronics industry, with all communications carried out by computers. It was the unanimous conclusion that the present work force and the young work force involved in these communications will have to be retrained. We will have to have a revolution in training methods leading up to employment.
We will have to do the same thing with much of our conventional industry that must acquire recruits. Why is it that we cannot get any skilled tradesmen and craftsmen in Alberta for love nor money? Money cannot buy them. The training programs are such that young people who have not been motivated the right way are not prepared to spend their time learning a trade. People are not prepared to transfer from other parts of Canada in the large numbers that are needed. People own homes where they are and, if they move, to whom can they sell them?
There is definite immobility, except in the absolute socialist heaven where worker number one is moved to place number 101 and the worker who is at place 102 is moved back to being worker number two. Everyone becomes a tool of the state. That is true socialism. One cannot expect a person just to pick up and move today because there has to be a job at the end of the line. That is not enough. There are many other factors. But the error has been with our provincial departments of education both at the secondary and the advanced level. The department of manpower has to share the blame. Then, of course, there is the cockeyed unwillingness to admit that persons who have trained abroad will be as well trained as persons here.
