There is difficulty in getting equivalent certificates, even between provinces. For instance, the bricklayer from Britain has a great deal of difficulty getting accreditation here in Canada. The carpenter from Austria or Germany is not admitted as a certified craftsman. Then there are the plasterers, the tile setters and all of those tradespeople who know that these trades were not developed here.
Therefore, these are artificial barriers to the movement of the trained personnel we need. All of this is part and parcel of the philosophy of this bill. To simply say that we will set up some sort of bureaucracy or compensation board with officials, and all that the individual worker will have to do is to make application in a certified industry, is not good enough. The worker is not protected if the industry is not a certified or designated industry. Perhaps there would be a provision that there shall be 50 persons laid off or 10 per cent, whichever is the lesser, but certainly there has to be a floor; otherwise a person who loses his or her job for one reason or another could go running to this compensation board and say: "Here, I have been laid off; I want the state to support, compensate or retrain me, but at public expense".
That should not be part of it at all. I suggest that the problem highlighted by the objective of this particular bill is contributed to by a number of causes. First is the improper training of our young work force. Second is the non-existence of facilities for retraining workers. Can those people who maintain they have some connection with the work force tell me which provinces have adequate training facilities for adult workers to retrain sufficiently to meet standards set up in other provinces, enabling the worker, either male or female, to get a job in a field where their labour is required?
How many provinces are set up that way? How many trade unions have participated in that type of planning? How many trade unions would permit the retraining and introduction of workers without insisting they go through an extensive apprenticeship program, apprenticeship programs open only to 16 or 17-year-olds? An area in which there is great difficulty today is the retraining of workers and an acceptance of retrained workers in new industries, particularly if they are organized from institutions such as the Alberta Vocational Retraining School. Why cannot these people be accepted as fully trained and accredited workers without going through prehistoric and impossible apprenticeship plans? Those are the problems we face.
What about those provinces which have sort of down-home legislation which says local workers only need apply. Whether trained or otherwise matters not. If there are not trained workers, it still does not matter. It is a dog in a manger situation. There should be the ability to move from one end of Canada to the other if one so desires. But that is not possible.
How many new industries would have been able to get started in this country without help from outside? What about the people from Saskatchewan who went to work in the Alberta oil industry, the Americans who came to Alberta when Canada did not have any oil workers of its own? What about pipeline welders? There was a time when there was not a
welder in any province who could touch a pipeline. We talk about building pipelines here and there across the country. Most of the provinces do not have standards even for pipeline welders. That is how far behind in history the provinces are. They are behind in their planning, engaging in restrictive thinking all the time. At the same time these self-same provinces are the ones that impose restrictions on the movement of workers from other provinces who are qualified to do a particular job.
This bill is a palliative. It is the ultimate solution for those people who cannot be accommodated through retraining. I would much rather see a worker retrained and replaced in a productive job than become the subject of benefits under this particular bill. This may not meet the views of certain members, but Mr. Speaker, I come from an area where employers are denied workers. They advertise nationally and through the Canada Manpower employment service. There is absolutely zilch in return, or the few occupants are either has-been's, incompetents, rub-a-dubs or what have you who cannot hold the job or perform. Then when we want to get some people from the Orient or Europe who are qualified, we are told no, and it takes a year to process a worker coming from abroad. Those people are highly trained, often far better trained than our people. They are motivated and make responsible citizens. Gracious me, my grandparents, and possibly the grandparents of half the people now in this chamber, came to this country under similar circumstances.
To let somebody come into this country today from abroad is nonsense, according to the Department of Employment and Immigration as well as to a lot of other sectors. We have many people who are institutionally unemployed. This is built in through unemployment insurance, welfare and inadequate training. There is no possibility of employing them in the skilled trades where they are required. First, there are no schools for them to attend if they wanted to be retrained and, second, many would not want to move.
What happens? The employer in the area where the workers are required faces inadequate production with a resulting loss, and everything becomes more costly, yet there are thousands upon thousands of people who want to work if given a chance and if there were adequate training facilities for them. If that were the case, I think we could see some possibility of reaching the day when the Canadian work force could respond to our needs. According to the figures, there is a work force surplus of 890,000. That figure is artificially stimulated by other factors. Many of those people are not genuinely out of work, and there are hundreds of thousands of jobs available in the country. These people either cannot get to those jobs or they could not perform them even if they wanted to. That is one of the hard facts of life. It is regrettable that we have so many people who would like to work but cannot because they are not trained to do the work that is available.

The fact that geographic designation is permitted or required by this legislation and the ILAP legislation, in my view, builds in some structural difficulties that will have to be corrected. This is one of the reasons why I wanted to speak for a few minutes today.
I indicated that my riding is adjacent to the city of Windsor and its environs which enjoy designation. The fact is that by that designation some several millions of dollars can be made available to industries which want to relocate in the Windsor area, making work available for those persons who have been disrupted by reason of the automotive industry's downturn. The fact is that by geographic accident those communities which find themselves outside the designated areas and yet are providing work for people who have been laid off now find themselves competing for additional funding with which to attract new industry.
Let me give you an example. The town of Kingsville, located 35 kilometres outside the designated area of Windsor, has a number of parts industries located in it. They have suffered, as have many other small communities around the area, because of the loss of markets in the automotive industry, and many people have in fact been laid off. While the downturn was taking place, the mothers and fathers in the community, recognizing that something was coming in terms of the automotive industry, attempted to provide industrial parks. They brought people from abroad as well as from other parts of Canada attempting in this way to attract potential industry by communicating to them the benefits of locating in the town of Kingsville. They now find themselves competing with the industrial commission for Essex County and Windsor not on an even footing because an additional tool has been given to the designated community which they do not have. In my view that puts them at a disadvantage, and the minister will know I

have attempted to make that point with him and his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), under whom ILAP comes.
Contrary to arguing, as those who have spoken before me have done, that the program is wrong and, because it does not do all things for all people, it should be thrown out, I would suggest that it needs modification to enlarge the designated areas or, at the very least, to include those persons working in a designated industry who find themselves dislocated, regardless of where they are located geographically.
We find that what results is a silly arrangement under which persons from the city of Toronto who, because they work in and choose to commute to Windsor, find themselves designated in the industry and entitled to the benefits. I think the program is good but I think it is unfair when looked at in terms of those kinds of circumstances. What we have to do is to modify the program to take care of the circumstances I have talked of so that it follows more closely the spirit of this bill and removes some of the blemishes, as I described them, that I am able to perceive from having experienced them.
The principle is correct. Undoubtedly, we have many Canadians over the age of 55 who are working in a particular industry experiencing an economic downturn and who will never be able in practice to find other employment. I do not think there is any member in the House who would not want to assist those people. They are not the kind of people whom the hon. member for Edmonton West described as no-gooders, bums and what-have-you. These are people who have worked for 30 and 40 years only to find themselves caught in circumstances out of which they cannot extricate themselves. I would not expect the hon. member to suggest that people in those circumstances should not be given assistance. Indeed, I would hope that he would join me in saying that we should do as much as possible to assist them.
I believe that is what the minister is trying to do through this bill. All I am inviting the minister to do is to try to do a little more for those whom I have described to him, people who, because of the way the bill is drafted, are excluded from receiving any benefits under the provisions in this bill. If it can be done either here or at the committee, I will be overjoyed. If we cannot do it, I have used this opportunity to advise the minister that even if the rose is beautiful, there are some blemishes on it that we should try to clear up.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to speak in support of Bill C-78 because I think it is an innovative and sensitive bill. The bill focuses on a group of people who are forgotten in this particular era. The people affected are between the ages of 54 and 65. Having worked with these people and having been responsible for the care of many of the workmen in this particular age group, I have found them to be a very special and vulnerable group at work and in society. They are people who have committed themselves to long hours of work and who have done so with great expertise and dedication. But in that particular period of their lives, age creeps up quietly upon them. It does it in a way that is difficult to perceive. It is difficult to attribute a certain weakness of health that goes with advancing years to any illness. This is something that is inherited and that deteriorates and makes their bodies more vulnerable to the work they do. There are no set rules or any real understanding of that process. It is a process that is present in each and every one of us and that manifests itself very insidiously and in a way that is difficult to attribute to any particular factor. Often these same people do repetitive work. They perform work that
Labour Adjustment Benefits
appears not to be traumatic or that would ordinarily cause any defects or trauma to the body. But regardless of what work you perform, if you do it repetitively and continuously over a long period of time, evidence of some wear and tear and deterioration starts to appear. I am sure if we were to study the vocal chords of a good percentage of the hon. members, we would find very definite changes. If we were to study another part of their anatomy, we would find that prolonged sitting has an effect on the vascular system in that particular part of their bodies. This happens to every individual who does repetitive work.
These changes, that are so difficult to identify readily, lead to some deterioration in the physical fitness of that person, so that he is no longer able to compete in his work world with younger people. In time these people imperceptibly become disabled-although they are not ready to admit it-but they cannot submit claims to the Workmen's Compensation Board. As a result of their dedication over the years, they have reached the stage where they can no longer compete with the industrial world.
I feel this bill is focused on that particular group of people. It is one of the first pieces of legislation where attention has been directed to them and their plight understood.
I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who indicated that many of these people should not be considered as requiring benefits, but provision should be made to retrain them in other aspects of the work. Their expertise should be utilized in apprenticeship programs. They could be a model to young workmen. A concentrated effort to use their talents should be made.
The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) remarked on the use of robots. Again I see no real criticism of that. Time and again robots and machinery of that sort are used in areas that are unliveable, areas where people would have to work under conditions where there is a high concentration of chemicals and where repetitive activity adds to the rapid deterioration of certain tissues. I think robots fulfil the need in that particular field. It must be remembered that working with robots requires the acquisition of new skills for the new technology. The maintenance of these structures come into play. If they were utilized intelligently and prudently, they would add to the safety and comfort of the worker. But again a price must be paid, and that price is that some jobs will be lost in a particular way.
I want to conclude by referring to a statement which was once made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in which he indicated that the Liberal government does not worship either productivity or growth; it works for the people. I believe this bill is eminently consistent with that philosophy.

Of that I am absolutely convinced.
I stood in the House earlier today during question period. I think my question was relevant to the bill before us. This piece of legislation proposed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) is supposed to help Canadians who are laid off. Perhaps it behooves us to identify these Canadians. To a large extent they are men or women who have provided loyal, productive service to an employer for an extended period of time. I told the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), who is a supporter of the high interest policy which is producing these lay-offs, that scientific evidence indicates clearly and unequivocally that when unemployment rates increase, the number of people who will suffer ill health increases. He stood up and said that it was nonsense. That told me something about the state of knowledge and the state of caring in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and in the cabinet generally. They say one thing and do another.
When I asked the minister the question, I had in my hand a study by Professor Brenner from Sir Johns Hopkins University. The figures presented by Dr. Brenner suggest that when there is a 1.4 per cent increase in the unemployment rate, social and health consequences follow. Coincidentally, this 1.4 per cent is very close to the increase in the unemployment rate in the last 60 days. It does not include the lay-offs announced this week, last week and the week before; they were massive. We will be looking at a 9 per cent unemployment rate when the next set of figures comes out. It will amount to well over one million Canadians, and there will be consequences.
I should like to read some figures into the record. Suicide is predicted to rise 5.7 per cent with a one per cent increase in the unemployment rate. Instead of 100 people committing suicide this month in Canadian cities, it will be 106. There will be something like an 8 per cent increase in the homicide rate, an 8 per cent increase in the number of people who will be murdered because of the increase in unemployment in the last 60 days. Last November, almost a year ago, some figures were provided by the Canadian Council on Social Development to all members of the House, including the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. They indicated that somewhere between 9,000 and 10,000 people in the coming 12 months will die because of the increase in unemployment. When one has devoted a significant chunk of one's life to productive service to an employer for the production of goods and services which we all need and value, and suddenly society says, "You are laid off; you are no longer useful", it throws the individual and his family into a crisis. It is the kind of crisis people find very difficult to deal with. They bottle up their feelings, they do various things with them, but the consequence is scientifically demonstrated to be an increased need for things like health care funding. The budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) of a year ago indicated that he intended to cut out $1,500 million worth of social spending related to hospitals, medical care and retraining for people who are laid off. We have a policy which is throwing people out of work. Yet it is accompanied by a policy in which health care funding will not be increased but will be decreased. They will throw people out of work, they will give them heart attacks, but there will be no available hospital beds. This is the reality of Liberal policy. It is a translation of highfaluting statements about a just society and caring about people.

when you create wealth, you have something to share with the unfortunate people in society. You just do not talk about it a great deal; indeed, you do not have to talk about it because you can do it.
If any member of this House were faced with the prospect of a lay-off, or an extended period of drawing unemployment insurance-and most members of this House have never been in that position-he could ask himself what comfort glowing phrases and lovely words are when his kids are hungry or he cannot afford to let them go to the skating rink, when his wife is worried or when he seeks to escape his problems with a bottle. That is a consequence for the one million Canadians who are unemployed today. That is a potential consequence for the several thousand people who have been laid off in this country this week, last week and the week before that.
When I examine this piece of legislation, I cannot get rid of the image of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce standing in this House earlier today. When I asked him what he was going to do about the health victim that the government's economic policy is creating, he laughed. Many members of his party laughed as well. They seemed to say, "It is not a serious problem. We don't care about the health victim of economic policy. That is nonsense." "That is nonsense," the minister said. It is not nonsense, Mr. Speaker. It is a scientific fact. The scientific fact translates into real people, people who are having those heart attacks, those marital breakdowns, people who are going to jail because their way out of distress is to do something illegal. Those are the real consequences of the kind of economic policy that we have had for far too long in this country.
Do hon. members opposite not care? I find that hard to believe. I meet those hon. members in the halls and I know that many of them do care, but far too often they do what they are told instead of what is right. Far too often they are not encouraged to look at the words and the consequences of those words.
I skimmed through this bill earlier today, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps after two years I am becoming sensitive to certain themes. Those themes run through bill after bill that we consider in this House. I find them disturbing and not in the best interests of Canadians and Canadian society.
One theme which runs through almost every bill brought forward by cabinet to this House is that we will have some kind of board or commission. Two things are wrong with a board or commission, Mr. Speaker. The first is that the minister appoints the people who will serve on it, and the second is that the minister and the cabinet determine the amount of money the members should be paid. Just once I should like to see a piece of legislation come into this House which would provide for the appointment of a board or commission but would stipulate that the appropriate standing committee of this House would conduct a public inquiry into the background and competence of the people to be appointed, and that Parliament would control the amount of money to be paid for their services. If that were done then we, the elected representatives of the people sent to this chamber, could be
Business of the House
helpful in screening appointments to make sure that the people selected to serve on a board or commission had the background, the value systems and the professional credentials adequate for the job.
That kind of principle has never been contained in a piece of legislation brought forward by the cabinet to this House in the two years that I have been here. Instead, the minister shall decide who shall serve and the minister shall decide how much they shall be paid.
We are often amazed when we see the names published in The Canada Gazette. Regardless of the board, or commission the members are frequently defeated Liberal candidates or Liberal campaign managers. It is as if performance in that one function, serving the Liberal Party of Canada, were the primary and only qualification required to make the kinds of decisions about people's lives that the board or commission provided for in Bill C-78 is going to be asked to make.
This commission will be asked to sit in judgment on individual Canadians. If you are laid off, then you will have to be in a designated industry or a designated region before you are eligible to apply for benefits. That designation comes, basically, from cabinet. If you live in a Liberal cabinet minister's riding, then you are more likely to be designated than if you do not. Everybody's tax dollars are involved but people are not treated equally from coast to coast. Whether you are deemed eligible will depend upon where you live. The cabinet minister's campaign manager will probably be head of the board, and you will have to provide that person with any piece of information requested. There will be no secrecy or no concern for your rights. The board can compel you to give information. Then that person may sit in judgment, and you will get your $100 or $150 per week or you will not. One person will and the other person will not.
Is that the kind of system that we as Members of Parliament believe to be in the best interest of Canadians?

He said: Mr. Speaker, first may I say that this bill has been before the House on a number of occasions in the past. I have been the sponsor in its present form. Other motions have been made in past years concerning the Commissioners of Internal Economy. I have moved in a period of transition with this bill. If hon. members have any idea of the management, administration of the management and provision for members' services in this House, they will fully understand my motivation in putting forward this bill.
I want to make it patently clear that putting forward this bill, which ultimately has the Speaker delegate the Speaker's powers with regard to the administration of the Chamber, is absolutely no reflection upon the present or any previous incumbent of the Chair. It is a matter of principle. I have nurtured it ever since I was Speaker. In those years of many years ago, there was only one fifth or one sixth of the number of employees now on the strength of the House of Commons.
What I intend through this bill is that all matters of administration of this House be delegated to a committee of five commissioners. The number of commissioners would be expanded by one. The commissioners would come from the House generally and not be limited artificially, as they have been hitherto for some 114 years, to active members of the cabinet.
A few years ago, the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, as a result of a casting vote by one of your colleagues now in the chair, decided I was wrong in saying that commissioners could be members of the Privy Council wherever they sat in the House. All good authority was on my side, but the politics of the situation at that time was such that they could not agree with me. Be that as it may, what came out of those committee hearings was an advisory committee on management and members' services. That was only a small step forward. This House is governed by a system that is an anachronism in legislatures around the world as we know them.
It is my humble submission that the Speaker, in addition to being the official host on behalf of the House of Commons, has more than enough work for any super competent person. The role of the Speaker should be limited directly to this chamber and to that which is appurtenant to it, such as Hansard and the committees. In my view, we should not, as the present management committee has decided to do, hive off Hansard, the committees branch, and the clerks under the Administrator. I think that is a shocking decision. I have said so publicly, and I repeat it publicly.
As I said, my bill would amend the House of Commons Act by naming a fifth commissioner, a person who, like the others, need not be a member of the cabinet. He or she could be an active member of the cabinet. As a formula I would suggest that one of the ministers of state, perhaps a junior minister, could be named a commissioner and that person designated as the chairman of the Board of Internal Economy. The bill would provide, if the government and possibly the majority of
House of Commons Act
the House saw fit, for a representative on the board who had a direct link with the cabinet. We are practical people. I think it is good in that way to have somebody who can act as liaison with the cabinet.
The position of the Speaker as a commissioner is not abolished by the bill. The Speaker by my bill delegates his or her powers to one of the other persons, who is to be chairman of the committee. It is a formula, but in principle it seems to me that we still have to have the Speaker as head of the House of Commons. Even though the Speaker is head, it does not mean that his or her powers cannot be delegated. This delegation of power takes place at Westminster.
It was a strange thing but until a few years ago the monarch, either the king or the queen, was actually the head of the palace of Westminster. The powers of management and so forth were exercised on behalf of the monarch through the Speaker. That power was turned over from the monarch to the Speaker, and now the Speaker in turn has delegated many of the Chair's powers, or obligations, to members of the management committee. The Speaker can still participate because the Speaker has not yielded his or her position as a commissioner.
With regard to the administration of this chamber, I would say that there are now about 3,200 or 3,300 employees who come under the direct umbrella of the jurisdiction of the Speaker. The organization is now much more complex. When I was Speaker 20-odd years ago-and one hates to refer to a time that long ago-there was one building under the Speaker's jurisdiction, with a second one coming on strength. The West Block came on strength shortly after I yielded office to my successor, Speaker MacNaughton. Now the West Block, the East Block, the Confederation building and the Wellington building are all under the aegis of the Speaker. There are many ancillary areas which, as one who served as a Speaker, I feel take up far too much time and energy of the Speaker today. I refer specifically to this sapping administration. Even with the best will in the world and with competent officials to assist the Chair in the discharge of those duties, too much time and energy is demanded of the Chair, to the detriment of the discharge of the actual duties of the Chair.
There is one point on which I will be critical. I do not think the Speaker occupies the chair enough. The position of presiding officer is, immediately after question period, turned over to a series of assistants or deputies. The Speaker returns to the chair only to preside over formal votes. I suppose the Speaker would have to come back into the chamber if there were an appeal from one of the assistant Speakers.
It is my view that the Speaker should be in the chair much more often. I think the four assistants who normally occupy the Chair are involved in a further anachronism. They preside at all second reading debates, all report stage debates and all third reading debates. When a bill comes to a vote, the Speaker is in the chair. However, these assistants or deputies after having exercised the role of a presiding officer immediately turn around to vote. In my opinion, that is totally wrong. The Speaker is precluded by the rules from voting except in the case of a tied vote. There is no question about the fairness

of a member of this House occupying the position of the Chair, but the rules say that that person shall not be entitled to vote. Nothing is said about the deputy chairmen, deputy or assistant speakers. They may profess to be the most fair-minded people in the world, but why are they not treated the same as the Speaker and not allowed to vote? But then we would hear the cry that far too many people from the government side could not vote. But why not follow what the Mother of Parliaments does? Deputy speakers are chosen equally from either side of the House.
All the brains are not located on the government side of the House. The same goes for the presiding officers of the House. Therefore if we followed the practice of Westminster, we would have a better balance. With my bill, I am not only getting a better balance in the administration of the House by naming people to the commission who are closer to members because cabinet ministers who are commissioners are busy men. It is very difficult to get them into meetings. At the present time I understand they have meetings at least once in three weeks. I have known the situation to go four or five months before the Speaker could dragoon those cabinet ministers together at one time over lunch. Those commissioners who came to decisions received their advice and instruction from the Speaker.
I can assure you, as an original member of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services, that that practice is most frustrating, and it is wrong in form. The chairman of that committee should be along as an adviser, but he is never invited to these meetings. I think he should be. The services and the management of this House are for the members. The four commissioners as provided for in the House of Commons Act is an anachronism from 1867. They were the only Members of Parliament who remained most of the time in Ottawa. At one time members sat in this House for very short periods. Today we have a year round operation and there is no reason in the world why a senior member of the New Democratic Party, senior members of the two major parties should not be commissioners. It should not necessarily be done on the basis of party strength. There are men with greater knowledge and ability who could be administering services here, negotiating with staffs and arranging for clearances of grievances and all that sort of thing, which should be in the hands of this committee of members, numbering either five or seven.
The ultimate purpose of my bill is that the administration of this House shall effectively be in the hands of the members of this House and not in the hands of absentee landlords such as the Commissioners of Internal Economy are, commissioners with whom ordinary members have no direct contact except by buttonholing them, and that is the wrong type of influence.
I invite hon. members to examine my proposal and I would hope to see the bill, or the subject matter if so desired, sent to the appropriate committee so that we can take a look to see if we can design a formula which I in my experience of over 25 years in this House feel would be far more preferable for
members than is the present system, even though the function is being discharged by people of the greatest goodwill. The system and the format works against them. I would suggest that my bill be accepted, read the second time and sent to the committee at five o'clock this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy this afternoon to have an opportunity to participate in this debate. First, I want to congratulate the hon. member for bringing forth this private member's bill. I certainly believe it to be a step in the right direction and I too hope it will go to the committee to be discussed in more detail, with hopefully some form of it being enacted by this Parliament.
We are elected to this House of Commons, just as any minister who sits in this place is elected, with the same rights and privileges, we are told, and with the same responsibilities to our constituencies. It is true that a minister may have a larger constituency than individual backbench members, as they are called, but I submit that we are also told we have a duty to the country. I do not think anybody would suggest other than that each elected member of this chamber has a duty to the country as a whole. If we are responsible enough to be elected by our constituents, just as are the ministers, then I see no reason that backbench members of this House should not sit on the Board of Commissioners of Internal Economy.
I am not even sure, however, that the hon. member is going far enough in his proposal to change the Board of Commissioners. I am not sure that that Board of Commissioners should not be abolished altogether and the role taken over by what is now called the Advisory Committee on Management and Members' Services.
If I may, staying within the principles of the bill, talk for a minute about committees, I would like to do so. It would do little good, I suspect, to abolish the Board of Commissioners and replace it by a committee structured as is the present Committee on Management and Members' Services, or almost any of the other standing committees of the House. The committees of this House are too big and unwieldy. They have no real power, as they should. They have the opportunity generally to react to something that is already government policy. They have no policy input, as they should. In order to accomplish that, it seems to me those committees must be made much smaller than they are today.
If we had a Management and Members' Services Committee consisting of seven members of this House, elected on a pro rata basis among the parties, without suggesting that any party should have to split a member in order to have exact representation, I think such a committee could function well, not only in the interests of the economy of the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada, but as well in the interests of the real needs of members representing their constituents and carrying out their legislative work here in the House of Commons.
The time has come when backbench Members of Parliament
must not only have and take but must demand a much larger
November 6, 1981

role in policy formulation. With the evolution of society and the complexity of modern social, economic and other problems, the administration of government has grown much faster than the House of Commons, much faster than the Parliament of Canada. I am not advocating that this House should grow much larger, but I am advocating that the members who sit in this place should have a great deal more to say than they now have about what happens here, and that means a very drastic change in the Standing Orders of this House.
This is one of the things for which I have been agitating since the end of my first year here. It is one of the things we are promised with every new session of Parliament, but it is one of the things that has never been accomplished. It is my hope, and I have some faith that it will be fulfilled, that in the next session of Parliament we will take a comprehensive look at the Standing Orders of this House. I suggest that when that is done we should also take a comprehensive look at how this place itself is managed.
One of the subclauses of this bill suggests that the Speaker have the power to delegate any or all of his or her administrative powers to the commissioners. I have some difficulty with that. 1 believe we must always retain the Speaker of this House as the guardian, the protector and the ensurer of the rights and privileges of the members. The Speaker of this House is not above the other members of this House; the Speaker of this House is the first among us, and in fact in this House no member should be above any other. However, the Speaker must be responsible, in the final analysis, for the administration of the Parliament of Canada and for the protection of the rights and privileges of its members. If the Speaker is to delegate all of his or her authority, I have some difficulty in determining how the Speaker is to fulfil that role. That is a role I do not want to see taken from the Speaker.
We have many problems in this House. We have a problem as a result of every member being treated as though he or she represented an urban riding. It is obvious that the needs of members representing rural ridings may be quite different from the needs of members representing urban ridings. When I talk about needs I am talking about the necessity for staff here and for staff for constituency offices. The manner of staffing those offices may be very different in rural areas and in urban areas. I have a riding, for instance, which covers some 5,500 square miles. It is about 150 miles in length. Obviously that is quite different from the riding of Spadina, for instance, or Edmonton West.

speechtext:
The people made a choice in Spadina, and I have no argument with that. That is the basis of our democratic system.
1 am afraid the basis of our democratic system is not always adhered to in this place. I think, for instance, of question period. It is virtually impossible for a backbench member on the government side of the House to get a question during
House of Commons Act
question period. Members are not always equal in this place. I understand there are quotas, and I do not blame the Speaker for that. Those are conventions which have grown in this place over the years. They are conventions which I believe are dangerous to basic democracy.
As I said earlier in my remarks, each of us has the same responsibility toward those who elect us. I have a great deal of difficulty in trying to justify to my constituents that I have not the same right and the same opportunities in this place to ask a question as does the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), for example. He just happens to sit on the other side of the House. It seems a very serious disadvantage to me when compared to the other members in the House. I want to reiterate that I do not blame any individual, only the fact that over the years conventions seem to have become regulations or rules, and I do not think that is right.
The hon. member for Edmonton West said we are governed here by a system that is an anachronism. I agree with him. In fact, I am beginning to believe that this whole place is an anachronism. The rules, our Standing Orders, are an anachronism, and it is high time the rules of this place were brought into the twentieth century. It is high time we had a legislative calendar such as the legislative bodies in other democratic countries have. It is high time we stopped sitting during the kind of nonsensical hours we do. We should have a reasonable schedule so we can plan our work and have sufficient time in our offices to deal with our constituency problems.
Much of the debate that goes on in this House, Mr. Speaker, is quite useless. It accomplishes nothing.
If committees were restructured and reduced in size to a maximum of 11 members and if the membership on those committees were made nearly permanent so that members do not play musical chairs in committee, we would be able to do very meaningful work there.
The government of the day should be willing to refer to committees substantive matters in the form of proposals rather than policies so those people who are formulating a particular policy can be called before a committee to justify the choices they might put before a minister. This should not be done when these policies have been carved in stone and have become pieces of granite which are known around here as bills. It becomes virtually impossible to change a policy once it is written in a bill and presented to the House. Unfortunately, that is about the only time it is referred to a committee, after it has been presented to this House as something which is already untouchable.
The voting system in this House is another anachronism. My colleague, the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen), brought this up earlier today during question period. 1 heartily endorse what he said. It would be a little nostalgic but there is something to be said, of course, for members having to stand in their place and vote because each member is standing up and accounting himself to the people who elected him. However, Mr. Speaker, when we have a situation such as we had last night where even when the votes had been grouped we had very repetitive actions taking place in this House, it is of no

November 6, 1981
House of Commons Act
value to our society or democracy. There is no longer any justification for Members of Parliament, who have finally reached the point where they are getting paid a reasonable salary for the work they do, spending their time jumping up and down in the House like jacks-in-the-box to record their vote. There is a better way, and it is not beyond the ingenuity of mankind to make that possible in this chamber. It is time it was done.
I would like to see a body of some kind, which is responsible to the members of this House, which would administer this place under the direction of the Speaker.
I have seen, in the short time I have been here, the evolution of the administration of this place to a point which I do not like very much. I do not wish anybody to confuse what I am about to say with personalities. 1 am talking about the structure and not about individuals. We have a position now, Mr. Speaker, in our House of Commons known as that of the Administrator. My recollection of the Senate and House of Commons Act is that it says that this place will be administered by the Speaker and that the Speaker can delegate authority to the Clerk and to the Sergeant-at-Arms. I have no recollection of this act ever being amended to include the position of Administrator. I am concerned at the growth of bureaucracy in this institution. I am concerned that the real authority, the real responsibility and the accountability for the administration of this place is going to fall into the hands, if it has not already done so, of non-elected people. That, in my opinion, is wrong.
I, for one, am going to insist that not only the government, but all members, continue to agitate, continue to insist that every member of this House, whether or not he is a Privy Councillor, is treated the same. All Members of Parliament should have access to government proposals, to government documents that are not already cast in stone, as I said earlier. I will insist, and I hope other members will, that the committee structure of this House be changed and that committees be made meaningful bodies of this House. They should have some authority, and if they do not, we are all wasting our time.
I am prepared, Mr. Speaker, to let the committee do its work for about one more year and if by that time nothing happens, if there are no changes, I will no longer attend it. I am not going to waste my time going through the farce that most standing committees are today.
I support the basic thrust of this bill and I hope it will go to committee so that it can study it and, hopefully, improve upon it and make some suggestions for reform of not only the administration of the House but of the structure of the organs of this House known as the standing committees so that the role of the Member of Parliament will have some meaning in this place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the most disturbing aspects of the Canadian parliamentary
system which is of course based on the British parliamentary system, is the extremely fuzzy line that separates the executive and legislative functions of the government. This is, of course, best illustrated by the fact that, strangely enough, both legislators and ministers sit in the House. I know that a long tradition has led to this anachronism, where in the House, for all practical purposes, the legislative and executive functions are mixed, and I am also aware that many of our constraints, such as the constraints of parties and the constraints of the government's collective responsibility are self-imposed, and that we are now in a situation where it is becoming increasingly difficult for members to show their independence. There are of course mechanisms outside the House through which members can express themselves, such as the caucus and similar opportunities for consultation.
However, since the early days of our parliamentary system, the situation has evolved to the point where members are, for all practical purposes, subject to extremely restrictive conventions. Do members realize, Mr. Speaker, that the administration of the House is under government control and that is exactly what it is, control. Only Cabinet members sit on the committee or council which administers this House at least as far as the budgetary function is concerned. This is quite extraordinary and totally unacceptable!
One of the first things that struck me when I came to this House, Mr. Speaker, was the realization that as members we had absolutely no control over our administration. None at all! This committee by which we are administered consists of ministers appointed by the head of the government. So we have here a legislative chamber that is actually administered by the government. Except for our tradition of democratic consultation and the rest, this procedure would certainly be applauded by regimes that go against everything we believe in. The sponsor of the bill under consideration referred to our world, and just now I was alluding to that other world to which I am sure no one here would very much like to go. The member is introducing Bill C-273, whose purpose is clearly to instil some common sense and, by broadening access to the administration committee, to give all members of the House an opportunity to sit on the committee and to make the division of powers meaningful. And I entirely agree on that. However, I find it unbelievable that at 4.45 p.m. we should be here dealing with a private bill so fundamental to our institution. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Miramichi refer to parliamentary reform. There are very many things to be done in that area, whether we concern ourselves with committees, votes, internal management or the conventional rules to which I referred a while ago and which virtually compel us on both sides of the House-and I am using a strong word, Mr. Speaker-to act as mere puppets as a result of standards imposed upon us. I think that the matter will require some consideration.
November 6, 1981

Have hon. members ever asked themselves, whenever a non-confidence motion as we call it is moved, generally by an opposition party, whether we are playing our role? We express confidence or non-confidence in the government but what about the other bills? What about the other bills where it is suggested that the question of confidence is also involved? Indeed when a minister's bill is rejected, the minister is assumed to have lost the confidence of the House as is the government and assuredly our colleagues opposite would be the first ones in such a case to rise and demand that the government resign and call an election. I have already said it. As parliamentarians we know how to impose unacceptable restraints. What is the true meaning of a non-confidence motion if everything we do here is related to non-confidence or confidence issues?
Now our entire concept and understanding of our own work as elected representatives to a legislative body are warped. We become locked into an impossible situation and it is no wonder, Mr. Speaker, that our constituents often cannot understand how we have managed to get ourselves into such a predicament. I am speaking of course in a general sense. It will surely take some time before we do agree to reconsider this way of thinking but perhaps it is time to start something. A parliamentary reform has been announced. You can be assured, Mr. Speaker, that the issue of confidence in the government will not be reconsidered. Perhaps it is too soon to do that as well. The hon. members on the parliamentary committee will debate the statistics or the figures and what their responsibilities ought to be. It will be suggested that the number of members be reduced. My colleague from Miramichi made an interesting statement: let us stop playing musical chairs.
You know, Mr. Speaker, never was I more embarrassed than I was two years ago, I think, when my party-I say that without false modesty-had taken a few members off the committee under the pretence that they were against a bill. I know that the system was so much different over there, and I do not necessarily advocate that system. One can imagine such a situation in the American Congress where the chairman would tell a member of the foreign affairs committee: "You know, you do not agree with me so you will have to be taken off the committee and replaced by someone else." But what are we, Mr. Speaker? Are we supposed to play our role as parliamentarians, as elected members, or simply sanction or legitimize, if you want-it is legitimate, be careful now, I am not saying that it is not legitimate, the government is elected of course and this House gives it its confidence and every four years it must undergo the electoral test, but in the day-to-day life, constantly legitimizing measures which are not necessarily in full accordance with what we think our role ought to be as elected members for a given region. And 1 am not saying that the government must fall, quite the contrary. I am simply saying that we should be able to play our role as elected members in a democratic way, and should the time
House of Commons Act
come when the government feels that perhaps it does not have the full confidence of the House because it has been defeated on a clause or on some sort of amendment or even on a bill, then the House, either the government itself or the opposition, may ask the House if the government still has its confidence.
If it has, then it can go on governing according to the wishes of the House as a legislative body. Therein lies the difference between the executive and the legislative levels. Why did we have to go through all this? To go back to Bill C-273, let us say that considerable progress has been made. When I was first elected to the House, there was not even a committee on management and members' services. We had no official spokesmen to voice our aspirations and our rights as parliamentarians to management except through the Speaker. We found ourselves in the most awkward situation of having to go and beg the government for a few dollars to buy a typewriter for instance, or to obtain the kind of services we deemed important and essential to help us fulfil our duties and obligations to the electorate. Incredible! Do we or do we not have a sense of responsibility? In other legislatures or legislative assemblies, the system is different. For example, there is the quaestorial system. I know that my colleague opposite who sponsored this bill is aware of this system which is used in the French National Assembly. However, in France, members of the National Assembly elect their own administrators in proportion to the parties represented. Does this mean that these administrators throw open the coffers, spend wastefully and do not take their own responsibilities? Not at all. Just like the other members, they are accountable for their administration and if they do not perform properly, they are either rejected by their colleagues or denounced by the newspapers and the general public. If we are responsible enough to ask our voters to elect us, to sit in this House, to rise day after day, to vote on decisions which are very important for the future of our country-there were 30 votes yesterday-I believe that we are responsible enough to administer our own affairs.
I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that, in my opinion, there was no need for the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) to take such an initiative this afternoon. It is incredible that we should even be discussing this. All the members should unanimously rise to take in hand their own destiny as legislators. However, I am not saying that the government is to blame. I am not saying that the government has not managed the House well; that has nothing to do with it. I simply say that we should show a minimum of respect for the difference between the legislative function, for which we are here, and the executive function, which has of course a purpose and which operates on a different level. Mr. Speaker, we should at least be the masters of our own destiny in this House. This is why I approve the initiative of the hon. member for Edmonton West and why I hope that we shall put an end once and for all in a few months, when we undertake parliamentary reform, to something which is anachronistic, and I am

November 6, 1981
House of Commons Act
confident, or at least I hope, that the government will see to it that we can pursue this evolution which has brought us from a situation where we had no say in our administration to the present state of affairs, where we have an advisory committee which discusses matters of interest to the members of the House and which makes excellent recommendations which have indeed been approved by the Internal Economy Commission, so that we can take our destiny in hand as the final stage of this evolution. This would only be normal. As for the rest, as for my comments on parliamentary responsibility and government responsibility in the House, it is of course a much wider issue. I have used very strong words because I believe that it is time for us, as Members of Parliament, to reflect on this matter since, once again, we have put ourselves in this strait-jacket in which we operate, and it is up to us to get out of it.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF INTERNAL ECONOMY COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
I would like to thank the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for precipitating this discussion by bringing in this private member's bill. I know it is an issue that he is very familiar with and that he has spent many years working toward trying to improve the operation of the House with regard to matters of this nature. When we look at this issue, Mr. Speaker, I think it is necessary to look at how the Commissioners of Internal Economy came to have the jurisdiction that they have and where they came from.
The Commissioner of Internal Economy was established at the first session of Parliament. At that point, Mr. Speaker, Parliament met only a few weeks each year. Most of the employees employed by Parliament in those earlier days were mostly clerks and messengers who were employed on a temporary basis. They were employed for a few weeks or a couple of months at the most. Patronage was not unknown in those days; in fact, it was common and rather rampant. In 1867 and shortly thereafter it was desirable-and, as we all know that practice has long since died out and has become more or less extinct, at least at the federal level-that members from outside the Ottawa area, from more distant parts of Canada, should have jurisdiction over who was employed by Parliament on a temporary basis and who received these jobs. It was felt that to put this in the hands of members from the Ottawa area would be giving Jack the Ripper an Avon route. Perhaps it would result in some great injustices.
To protect Parliament in those days, the Board of Commissioners of Internal Economy was set up. The only members from outside the Ottawa area who were here all year round were cabinet ministers. In conducting research into the historical development of the existence of the Board of Commissioners of Internal Economy, I found that that seems to have been the rationale for the reason why they wound up doing the job they have been doing for so many years.
A few years ago, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, recognizing the immensely more complex administrative requirements of the House in the late twentieth century, recommended the creation of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services so that members, other than the Speaker and ministers, could participate in the administrative decisions of the House. I think it is fair to say that probably most of the best improvements in the administration of the House have originated from this committee.
I think it could be argued that the situation does need review. This committee often meets in camera and rarely reports to the House. This does not mean to say that the members on the committee are unaware of its deliberations or its advice.
Furthermore, it is important to bear in mind that the committee does not have any executive authority in law. It remains with the Commissioners of Internal Economy. The committee can review the situation and hold what discussions they feel are appropriate and make whatever recommendations they feel are appropriate. In the final analysis, they do not have legal authority. This is something that has rested with the Commissioners of Internal Economy and continues to rest with them.
An example that we might look at is the Senate. These days some people tend to view the Senate as a bit of an anachronism in many ways. I suppose that is an issue that can be argued. Perhaps the example of the Senate is worth looking into. When you look at the Senate, you will find that almost all the administrative decisions that are taken there are not taken by the Speaker or in camera or by a body that does not report to the whole House, but by a standing committee that is accountable to the Senate.
What is the result of this? In recent months there have been many rumours and allegations, some of them perhaps based on fact, others on fiction. There have been counterclaims about the administration and the machinations that go on in the House. Of course, we have the nation's gossip columnists. Many of the political columnists have had a heyday talking about the debates and internal dissension that have, in fact, occurred.
